title: Choosing a House Foundation: Pad, Strip, Raft or Pile?
desc: How pad, strip, raft and pile foundations differ, when each is used, the deciding factors, and why you should not choose a foundation by copying your neighbour.
summary: A plain-language explanation of the four common house foundation types, the factors that decide the choice, and mistakes homeowners often make.
body: p

The foundation is the “foot” of the house: it receives the entire load of the walls, columns, floors, roof, furniture and occupants and transfers it to the ground. If the foundation is wrong, no matter how well the upper part is finished, it may settle, crack or tilt. This article helps owners understand the common foundation types so they can discuss them with the design engineer, not to choose a foundation themselves.
h2
1. Four common house foundation types
ul
Pad foundation: each column base has its own foundation block. Commonly seen in low-rise houses with small loads and good, fairly uniform ground.

Strip foundation: the foundation runs as a long strip under a row of columns or under a wall, in one direction or crossing in two. It distributes load more evenly and limits differential settlement between columns compared with pad foundations.

Raft foundation: a single continuous slab spread under almost the whole house footprint. Used when the ground is fairly uniformly weak, the load is large, or when a basement requires waterproofing and resistance to groundwater pressure.

Pile foundation: uses piles (pressed precast concrete piles, bored piles and so on) to transfer load to a good soil layer deep below. Commonly used when the surface soil is weak, the house has many floors, or it is close to a neighbouring house and its effect must be limited.
h2
2. What factors decide the choice of foundation?
p
There is no “best” foundation for every house. The engineer weighs these together:
ol
Site geology: whether the good soil layer is shallow or deep, and whether there is mud, fill or groundwater veins. This is the most important factor.
Structural load: number of floors, type of slabs, roof, water tank, and whether there is a basement.
Neighbouring works: adjoining old houses with shallow foundations that may be affected by foundation excavation or pile pressing.
Construction conditions: access for pile-pressing or drilling rigs, a cramped site, the rainy season.
Overall cost: not only the foundation cost but also the cost of dealing with later settlement and cracks if the wrong choice is made.
h2
3. Mistakes owners often make
ul
Building the foundation “like the neighbour's house”: two adjoining plots can still have different geology, especially in areas that used to be ponds, paddy fields or filled ditches.
Cutting back the foundation to save money: the foundation is buried and very hard to fix once the upper part is built; saving here usually costs much more later.
Planning to add floors later but not telling the engineer: a foundation sized only for the current number of floors will not suffice when floors are added.
Not surveying or asking about the site's history before designing the foundation.
h2
4. What does the law require for house design?
p

Under Clause 2, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP, an owner may design a house personally only when it is at the same time under 3 floors, without a basement, with a total floor area under 250 m² and under 12 m high. A larger house must be designed by an organisation or individual with the relevant expertise and experience. Even when self-designed, design and construction must still comply with technical standards and regulations and ensure the safety of neighbouring works (Clause 1, Article 10). See also Designing your own house: when must you hire a designer?.
h2
5. What should owners prepare when working with the engineer?
ol
Provide the site's history: whether it was a pond, paddy field, dump, filled land or long-stable land.
State future needs: whether you will add floors, build a basement, install a large water tank or plant trees on the roof.
Ask the engineer on what basis the foundation was chosen: a geological survey or local experience; if there has been no survey, what the risk is.
Ask for clear foundation drawings and have the foundation base and foundation reinforcement accepted before concrete is poured.
p
If you are unsure about the foundation option for your house, contact Quan Construction to get engineers' advice based on the actual conditions of your site.
note

This article is for reference; every work needs to be surveyed and designed by a qualified person. The principles above do not replace the drawings, technical instructions and calculations of the structural engineer for each specific house.
